headline: Shamrock Rovers’ Rory Gaffney Retires from Professional Football at 36
standfirst: Shamrock Rovers striker Rory Gaffney has announced his retirement from football after suffering a season full of injury.
body:
Rory Gaffney’s last domestic appearance came in last year’s FAI Cup final where he scored a brace to win Rovers the double for the first time in almost 40 years.

He ends his career with five league titles in six years and scored 37 league goals at the Hoops in 143 games, followed by many European ties with his last appearance for the club being a UEFA Conference League match in December where the Hoops lost 3-1 against Hamrun Spartans to end their European campaign. Gaffney sits fifth in the all-time list of League of Ireland goalscorers in European competitions with eight goals.

Before this season began, Gaffney underwent procedures on his Achilles abroad but due to an infection, his recovery was interrupted resulting in him not being able to return to match fitness for the new season.

Rory Gaffney had spells abroad before coming back to Ireland to play for Rovers where he played with Cambridge United, Bristol Rovers, Salford City, and Walsall.

headline: LOI Roundup:
standfirst: Lilywhites earn huge derby spoils, Pats slip up in title chase & Cork edge closer to First Division glory.
body:
With the final round of fixtures only around the corner, there was twists and turns aplenty over the weekend in both divisions of the League of Ireland.

The Premier Division didn’t see any movement across the league table come the end of the weekend but it wasn’t without its dramatics.

The Louth derby didn’t disappoint as usual. With both teams under a poor run of form and a desperation for three points for contrasting reasons heading into the fixture, it was the experience and quality of the Lilywhites skipper Daryl Horgan that earned the bragging rights for Dundalk as he fired in a 90th minute strike from a free kick which earned his side all three points as it finished 3-2. It’s a huge booster for the Lilywhites as they travel to take on Derry City in the quarter final of the FAI Cup on Sunday, while Drogheda entertain Galway United on Friday in hopes of recreating their cup success from two years ago.

League leaders Shamrock Rovers travelled to the Brandywell and quickly found themselves two goals down on two occasions inside the first half as a rejuvenated Ellis Chapman bagged a brace for the Candystripes. But with their character questioned in recent weeks due to their European qualification nightmare, the strength in depth told for the champions as inspired substitutions in Will Fitzgerald Dylan Watts salvaged a point late on with the final score at three apiece. They face Shelbourne in the only Premier Division tie of the weekend on Friday looking strengthen their grip on top spot.

Looking to put the pressure on at the top of the table was both St. Patrick’s Athletic and Bohemians. However, the Inchicore side came to a roadblock in the form of Graham Coughlan’s Waterford who ran out 2-0 victors away from home, extending their unbeaten run to 10 games in all competitions. For Bohs however, they heaped more misery onto a Sligo Rovers side bottom of the table as a first half rout seen them ease to a 3-0 win in the fourth last game at Dalymount Park while leaving them just five points off top spot come the end of the weekend. Both Pats and Bohs will do battle at Richmond Park on Saturday in the tie of the round of the cup, while Waterford and Sligo will play out an interesting affair at the RSC.

The clash in mid-table between Galway United and Shelbourne also provided entertainment as a last gasp strike by the veteran Jimmy Keohane cancelled out Daniel Kelly’s effort to ensure the spoils were shared and leave John Russell still in search of his first domestic win as Shels boss.

In the First Division, Cork City edged ever closer to being crowned champions with a routine 2-0 victory over Wexford at Turners Cross, leaving them in the knowledge that a win next week away Bray Wanderers, who suffered defeat at Athlone Town, will see them officially out of reach.

Elsewhere, UCD played out a game of the season contender with Finn Harps as they ran out 5-4 winners at Belfield, setting up an interesting contest with Cobh Ramblers next weekend who also remain in the playoff picture following a 2-2 draw with Longford Town.

The midlands side host Kerry FC on Saturday with the Kingdom only two point of the playoff spots themselves after claiming Munster derby bragging rights over Treaty United with a 3-1 win.

headline: Kian McMahon-Brown signs for Shrewsbury Town on loan.
standfirst: The Ireland underage start will return to Burnley at the end of the season.
body:
![](img/articles/kian-mcmahon-brown/images-1-30da40.jpg)


Kian McMahon-Brown is set for his first taste of senior football after joining Shrewsbury Town on a season-long loan from Burnley.

The Ireland underage international put pen to a new deal at Turf Moor earlier this summer, and the Clarets have now sanctioned a move to League Two so the young attacker can start racking up men's football minutes.

McMahon-Brown has been among the standout performers in Ireland's underage ranks over the last couple of years, and his form was rewarded with a run in Burnley's first-team squad during pre-season.

He offers plenty of tactical flexibility too. Comfortable leading the line as an out-and-out No.9, he can just as easily play as a false nine or a No.10, and he has the game to drop into midfield when a side needs it.

A regular senior environment looks like exactly the right move at this stage of his development, giving him a proper platform to prove what he's capable of.
author: Jack Deane

headline: Jacob Devaney shines on Hibernian debut
standfirst: The Manchester United and Ireland midfielder has started his second professional loan spell
body:
![](img/articles/jacob-devaney-shines-on-hibernian-debut/jacob-devaney-scaled-9dcc47.webp)


Jacob Devaney was so good at St Mirren last season that going back to Manchester United's academy football was never really an option this year, so another loan was always the plan.

He's now joined Hibernian on loan for the 2026/27 season, off the back of an eye-catching pre-season with United.

He's due back next summer, having signed a new contract before going out on loan, at which point he'll be assessed for a possible first-team role at Old Trafford.

This weekend gave him about as good a start as he could have hoped for at Hibs, and United will be pleased with what they saw.

### **How Jacob Devaney got on for his Hibernian debut**

Devaney started for Hibs in a 2-1 win over Dundee, and the way he played suggests he won't be out of the side for a while.

The 19-year-old settled in straight away and dominated the midfield, looking a cut above everyone else on the pitch.

- 81 minutes
- 75 touches
- 67/71 passes completed (94%)
- 2 key passes
- 3 defensive contributions
- 1 tackle won
- 3/5 duels won
- 4 recoveries

You could see just how much Hibs needed him on the pitch — a minute after he was substituted in the 81st, Dundee pulled a goal back.

The Irish youth international is off to a flyer, and if he keeps this level up over a full season, he'll have a real chance of forcing his way into Michael Carrick's first-team plans.

Failing that, a Premier League loan looks almost inevitable if he keeps making the Scottish Premiership look this easy, just as he did at St Mirren.

### **Devaney will be a big talking point for United next summer**

There's no doubting Devaney's quality, and by the time he's back at United next summer, there'll be plenty of noise around him.

Carrick will want to weigh up where he fits into the squad, but if regular minutes aren't on offer, he'll be a wanted man elsewhere.

He already had interest from clubs across Europe this summer, and that's only going to grow if this season goes the way it looks like it will.

A £20-30 million price tag next summer wouldn't be a shock — not that United should be selling — but it shows just how highly rated he is, and why this season could turn Devaney into a genuine star.

Definitely one to keep tabs on as the season goes on.
author: Jack Deane

headline: Grow Your Own: Why LOI Clubs Must Back The Academy
standfirst: The League of Ireland is finally making serious money from young players. If that’s where the game is heading, why aren’t more clubs spending now to produce the next Mason Melia?
body:
![](img/articles/grow-your-own-why-loi-clubs-must-back-the-academy/51832bfd-4663-4304-9add-35d4d6b9bd40-120-ed9765.webp)

There was a time when a League of Ireland club getting six figures for a player felt like very good business.

Séamus Coleman left Sligo Rovers for Everton for a relatively modest reported fee. Dawson Devoy went from Bohemians to MK Dons for around £150,000. Eoin Toal left Derry City for Bolton for a similar sort of figure. Good deals, certainly, but rarely the sort that allowed a board to suddenly start thinking three or four years ahead.Then Mason Melia happened.

St Patrick’s Athletic agreed a deal worth around €1.8 million upfront for the teenager to join Tottenham. Shamrock Rovers then went higher again, agreeing a guaranteed fee of roughly €2 million for Victor Ozhianvuna to join Arsenal.

Their deals could reportedly climb beyond €4 million each through add-ons, while sell-on clauses give their clubs the chance to earn again later.

The two biggest transfers in League of Ireland history have one fairly important thing in common.

Neither club bought the player.

They developed him.

And the conversation around young League of Ireland players has changed with it.

It’s no longer just: **“How long do you reckon we keep him?”**

Someone normally has another question now. **“How much would you take?”**

That’s a much better problem to have.

But it also leaves Irish clubs with a fairly obvious question. **If academy graduates are becoming one of the best ways of making real money in this league, why aren’t we spending more now to produce the next one?**

## **You Have To Plant Something First**


![](img/articles/grow-your-own-why-loi-clubs-must-back-the-academy/6281a6bf-e4cd-409a-968a-862b1cf1f4a9-256-0d1c58.webp)

Academies aren’t free.

There are coaches, pitches, physios, gym programmes, analysts, transport and education to pay for. Not every teenager becomes a first-team player either. Plenty won’t get close.

But the economics are completely different to senior recruitment.

Spend €80,000 on an established player and you’re investing in one player. Spend that money improving academy coaching, facilities or contact hours and you’re potentially improving 20.

It’s a bit like planting an apple seed.

You don’t put one in the ground on Tuesday and start complaining on Friday because there’s no apple waiting for you. You give it time and, if you do it properly, eventually you’ve got a tree producing plenty of them.

Melia is one particularly valuable apple.

But he didn’t appear from nowhere.

By May 2025, 261 players had passed through the St Pat’s academy. 114 had represented Ireland at underage level, 84 had reached senior first-team football somewhere and 28 had played for Pat’s themselves.

The coaching numbers are even more revealing.

FAI figures put average academy contact time at around 230 minutes per week. Pat’s were providing approximately 450 minutes at U15 level and 705 at U17, more than three times the national average for their older group. That puts them on par with English Category 3 academies such as Bolton and Preston.

Mason Melia wasn’t produced because somebody in Inchicore discovered a magic cone drill.

They gave players more time to get better.
## **Development Doesn’t Mean Starting Kids Every Friday**


![](img/articles/grow-your-own-why-loi-clubs-must-back-the-academy/5a13172b-b3e6-4441-ae87-74c6e60e2fa7-120-55fd7b.webp)

This is where academy conversations can get a little silly.

Investing in young players doesn’t mean a manager should reach a relegation six-pointer and throw three 17-year-olds into the starting XI because somebody upstairs has discovered the phrase “player trading model”.

Managers still have to win football matches.

Senior football for an academy graduate doesn’t necessarily have to come at his parent club either.

Loans matter. First Division football matters. Twenty-five proper senior games can be worth considerably more than another year being brilliant at underage level.

Vinnie Leonard is probably the best example of what the pathway can look like when it works.

Before Ireland went to the 2025 U17 World Cup, that squad had accumulated more than 13,000 senior club minutes between them. Leonard alone accounted for just over 3,000, nearly a quarter of the total. He made his Dundalk league debut in October 2024, became an important part of their 2025 First Division promotion campaign, was named in the PFAI Team of the Year and then earned a move to Norwich City.

Not to mention his academy teammate, Sean Keogh, who was picked up by Brighton while Dundalk were in the First Division, earning the Louth Side around €150,000. He has since helped Brighton win the U21 Premier League title.

That’s the pathway clubs should be trying to build.

Academy football. Senior minutes. Proper responsibility. Performance. Then, if the player is good enough and the contract is right, a transfer.

And Leonard did most of that in the First Division. You don’t need to throw a teenager into a title race or Europe to develop him. Sometimes a promotion battle in Louth is more useful than another season being the best player in the under-20s.

That bridge between academy and first team should be part of the investment.

Otherwise you can spend six years developing somebody, get him to 18 and suddenly realise nobody has worked out what happens next.

And Ireland has plenty of catching up to do before that stage anyway.

The Government-backed Double Pass audit found only 4% of League of Ireland clubs had a full-time head of coaching, compared with 46% among clubs in comparable football nations. Not one LOI club had four or more full-time academy coaches. Among the benchmark countries, 36% did.

Only 23% of Irish academies had access to indoor facilities, against between 61% and 81% internationally. Comparable countries were also giving U16 to U21 players around two extra training sessions every week.

We’re already producing €2 million footballers from that.

You’d have to wonder what happens when the structures actually catch up.
## **This Isn’t Just A Dublin Thing**


![](img/articles/grow-your-own-why-loi-clubs-must-back-the-academy/d6e6ea78-89a5-484d-9994-2d013c8877e0-162-b9c540.webp)

The easy response is that Shamrock Rovers and St Pat’s can afford all of this.

They’re in Dublin, have huge recruitment areas and are operating towards the top end of Irish football.

So look at Sligo.

Owen Elding joined Sligo Rovers as a 12-year-old. In 2025 he scored 16 goals in 38 games in all competitions, including 12 in the league, won PFAI Young Player of the Year and was named Sligo’s Player of the Year. His league goals were vital as Rovers stayed up.

Then Hibernian bought him.

Sligo described the deal as an initial significant six-figure sum, with the potential to rise to seven figures, while a sell-on clause means they could benefit again.

That’s the bit clubs should really notice.

Elding didn’t just make Sligo money when he left.

He gave them goals first.

An academy graduate can help keep you up, win promotion or get you into Europe before anybody writes the cheque.

Then, if you’ve got the contract right, you get paid too.

Quite a useful employee.
## **So Where Does The Next €100,000 Go?**


![](img/articles/grow-your-own-why-loi-clubs-must-back-the-academy/c85e45a5-0cb6-4df7-b83b-0524bc45ec52-640-35a837.webp)

This is why the timing feels different.

Budget 2026 provided €3 million in multi-annual Government funding for League of Ireland academies. Yet the FAI had asked for €4.45 million, arguing that would allow every academy to employ at least three full-time staff.

Its longer-term ambition went further again, towards significantly greater annual investment and academies eventually generating enough transfer income to help fund themselves.

In other words, Irish football is starting to plant the tree.

The question now is whether clubs keep watering it.

Nobody is suggesting they stop signing experienced footballers. If you’re bottom in September, the 32-year-old centre-half with 300 senior appearances might be considerably more useful than an academy presentation telling you about 2029.

Sometimes that signing keeps you up.

But when the next €100,000 becomes available, the conversation shouldn’t automatically begin and end with the first-team squad.

Could it hire another coach? Increase contact hours? Improve facilities? Fund loans? Help regional players travel? Put longer contracts around the best prospects? Develop a player education programme?

None of those will have supporters refreshing Twitter at 11pm waiting for an announcement video.

But neither did the work that produced Melia.

There will be academy players who never make their club a cent. There will be mistakes, late developers and teenagers who leave for Europe before clubs see much return.

That’s football.

But Melia, Ozhianvuna and Elding are showing what happens when it does work.

So by all means, sign the 34-year-old midfielder coming home if he makes your team better.

Just don’t spend every spare euro making Friday night slightly easier and then wonder five years later why somebody else is selling the next €2 million footballer.

headline: Derry City vs Shamrock Rovers
standfirst: Can Derry bounce back from last weeks defeat to Bohs?
body:
**Derry City team news** 
Derry go into this one bruised after a 5-3 defeat away to Bohemians at Dalymount Park. Michael Duffy opened the scoring in the 34th minute and added a stoppage time penalty but Derry conceded five, including a Ross Tierney brace. 
James Clarke was sent off, so Derry will be without him for this one. 
Tyler Smith also got on the scoresheet on Friday and offers another attacking outlet.
The defeat leaves Derry 7th, with Waterford breathing down their neck in 8th, just a point back after beating St. Pat's.

 **Shamrock Rovers form** 
Rovers arrive as league leaders, four points clear of second placed St. Pat's, and with two games in hand still to play, this trip to Derry and a meeting with Shelbourne in Tallaght next Friday.
They're unbeaten in six **league** games, but they have lost their last 4 matches, a 5-1 defeat to Egnatia in Europa League qualifyibg, a 3-2 defeat to St. Pat's in the cup, and a 1-1 draw then a 1-0 loss over the two legs to Finland's KuPS, knocking them out of Europe.

The match kicks off at 4pm at the Brandywell, and you can watch the match live on loitv.

headline: Como Sign 17 year old Josh Harpur
standfirst: The Bohemians striker has played just 30 minutes of senior football.
body:
![](img/articles/misc/651746449-122205377540494928-61465439613-7c1d1d.jpg)
*Josh Harpur went on trial to Como in March. (reptracker)*

Cesc Fabregas’s Como have agreed a deal for Bohemians striker Josh Harpur on a 3 year contract, pending the completion of his medical.

The initial fee is thought to be around €250k.

The Cavan native only turned 17 yesterday, on the 27th of August.

Harpur is following the footsteps of Naz Raji and Liam Kerrigan who left the league of ireland to join Como in 2024 and 2022 respectively.
 Ultimately, both players found their opportunities restricted as Como grew too quickly, securing promotion to Serie A and bringing in elite talent that pushed the young Irish prospects down the pecking order. 
Both players have since left Como permanently, with Raji having returned home to Shamrock Rovers and Kerrigan now playing in the Serie C with AC Renate.

Harpur made his debut in Bohemian’s 7-0 win over Killester Donnycarney in the FAI Cup - he was only 15 at the time. 

Como are set to play PSG, Manchester United, RB Leipzig, FC Barcelona and Troy Parrot’s Real Betis in the Champions League this season, to name a few.

body:
![](img/articles/rocco-vata-to-italy-clubs/da483340-063a-11f0-853e-4d8e078f7eb4-47ac56.jpg) 
*Rocco Vata on his Ireland debut.*

Watford and Republic of Ireland attacker Rocco Vata is said to be wanted by both Roma and Bologna. 

Vata left his boy-hood club Celtic in the summer of 2024 to join Watford on a free.
In the two full seasons since then, he's made 53 appearances, scoring 6 goals - although the majority came in his first season, when he made 37 appearances. 
Injuries meant he only played twelve times in 25/26 and now he could be set to play Champions League football in Italy - according to Ben Jacobs (@JacbobsBen on X).

Vata was born in Glasgow and is elgible to play for Ireland through his Grandmother, he's also eligible for Albania and Montenegro.

His market value is currently around €1.8 million and his contract isn't set to expire until the summer of 2028.

headline: Shamrock Rovers’ Recruitment Model:
standfirst: Is It Time to Look Beyond Ireland?
body:
## Stephen Bradley built Ireland’s dominant side by mastering the domestic market. If Rovers want the Europa League next, they may need to look further afield.
![](img/articles/shamrock-rovers-recruitment-model-is-it-time-to-look-beyond-ireland/f98b269e-33ec-41f0-808a-96391fcf8c02-102-1fa4f7.webp)
Will Fitzgerald feels like a very Shamrock Rovers signing.

He was captain of Sligo Rovers, had been one of their most reliable players since arriving in 2022, could cover several positions and, most importantly, Stephen Bradley already knew him. Bradley had first tried to sign Fitzgerald years earlier and went back more than once before finally getting him this summer. There was no great mystery to solve. Rovers knew the player, knew the league and knew what they were paying for.

That has been a huge part of why Bradley’s recruitment has worked.

Look through the teams that have won five league titles in six seasons and you keep finding players who were already very familiar to anyone watching Irish football. Pico Lopes came from Bohs. Lee Grace from Galway. Gary O’Neill made his name at UCD. Dylan Watts had played for UCD and Bohs. Ronan Finn returned from Dundalk as one of the best midfielders in the country.

It wasn’t glamorous. It was just very good recruitment.

Rovers didn’t need somebody to explain whether those players could cope with the league because they had already watched them do it.

The question now is whether knowing Ireland this well is still enough for where they want to go next.

## **The Model Has Already Worked In Europe**

![](img/articles/shamrock-rovers-recruitment-model-is-it-time-to-look-beyond-ireland/fd0f2cf2-a395-423d-a64c-5d9b9deae9b6-102-a1f7da.webp)

There is a temptation after a night like Egnatia to decide Rovers need to change everything.

They don’t.

They were dreadful in Albania, losing 5-1 after travelling with a 3-1 first-leg advantage, and Bradley called it the worst performance he had seen from his team. Three days later, they let a 2-0 lead disappear against St Pat’s in the cup.

It was a bad week. It doesn’t suddenly make five league titles disappear.

It also doesn’t mean League of Ireland players cannot compete in Europe. Rovers have already proved the opposite. They reached the Conference League in 2022 and went much further in 2024/25, finishing 10th in the new league phase before beating Molde away in their knockout play-off. Michael Noonan was 16 when he scored the winner in Norway.

A side built largely from this league has already gone places Irish clubs are usually delighted to visit once.

So this isn’t about replacing domestic recruitment with a plane ticket and a Wyscout subscription.

It is about whether Rovers can add something to a model that already works.

## **There Is A Reason Bradley Is Cautious**

![](img/articles/shamrock-rovers-recruitment-model-is-it-time-to-look-beyond-ireland/d92f6f88-a0c7-42e8-bb46-2b31595a7eab-102-c4b5af.webp)

It is easy enough to say Rovers should start taking chances on players from England, Scotland or Scandinavia.


Bradley is the one who has to live with them if they are no good.

The League of Ireland has seen enough clubs spend money badly to make caution fairly understandable. Dundalk’s financial crisis in 2024 eventually reached unpaid wages and a genuine fear for the club’s survival. Foreign recruitment did not cause that collapse, but the whole episode was another reminder that ambition without enough control underneath it can become very expensive, very quickly.

Shelbourne are trying something different through their partnership with Jamestown Analytics, announced in January 2025. The idea is interesting because it gives them access to a much wider recruitment and analysis network, but it is still too early to say whether that model will consistently translate into better signings here.

There is no magic foreign market waiting to hand Irish clubs Champions League football.

Sometimes a player is available cheaply because you have found something everybody else missed.

Sometimes he is available cheaply because everybody else was right.

Bradley’s domestic-heavy approach takes some of that guesswork away. The case for widening it is not that he has been too cautious. It is that Rovers are now strong enough to survive the odd gamble.

## **Dundalk Already Found A Version Of It**

![](img/articles/shamrock-rovers-recruitment-model-is-it-time-to-look-beyond-ireland/bdc0aba4-d8e3-49a4-9a3b-d66ae821260b-184-2fbc4c.webp)

Stephen Kenny’s Dundalk are probably the best Irish example.

The side that beat BATE Borisov 3-0 in Tallaght in 2016 and reached the Champions League play-off was packed with players already known around the league. Sean Gannon, Chris Shields, Robbie Benson, Ronan Finn, Daryl Horgan and David McMillan were hardly hidden gems pulled out of nowhere.

Dundalk took good League of Ireland players and made a brilliant team.

Later, they added different profiles. Daniel Cleary had come through Liverpool and Birmingham City. Jordan Flores had been developed by Wigan. Will Patching had been with Manchester City and Nottingham Forest.

That is probably closer to the route available to Rovers now.

Keep taking the best players in Ireland when they fit. Keep developing the academy. Keep bringing Irish players home when the opportunity is right.

But also take a chance on one or two players who have spent years in professional academies abroad or are sitting in another small European league needing the right move.

Rovers do not need half a new squad every summer.

They might just need a couple of players they could not have found by watching Friday night football here.

## **Rovers Can Afford A Few More Risks**

![](img/articles/shamrock-rovers-recruitment-model-is-it-time-to-look-beyond-ireland/c59b1b05-6d51-4ebc-9b04-2898fb6458fd-102-adfad3.webp)

That is where modern Rovers are different.

The 2024 accounts showed a €1.183 million post-tax profit after a €2.365 million loss the year before. European football has brought serious money. Naj Razi moved to Como for an initial €450,000. Victor Ozhianvuna’s agreed move to Arsenal is worth around €2 million before potential add-ons.

They have Roadstone, an expanded Tallaght Stadium, a productive academy and a first-team squad good enough to keep competing for titles.

That gives Bradley a safety net most League of Ireland managers would happily borrow.

If Rovers sign a 20-year-old released by a Championship club and discover six months later that there may have been a reason he was released, Jack Byrne, Pico Lopes and the rest do not vanish overnight. Neither does the academy or the domestic scouting network.

And if it goes especially badly, there is usually a First Division club willing to help with the rehabilitation programme.

That is really where this argument lands.

Rovers should not move away from the League of Ireland market. It has been one of the main reasons they have dominated it.

But Bradley has already said the Europa League is the next target. Once that becomes the aim, recruitment has to stretch with it.

Rovers know Ireland better than anyone.

They might just need to know a few more places as well.

headline: LOI fixtures preview:
standfirst: Louth Derby takes centre stage while Cork City can wrap up First Division title.
body:
**It’s another big weekend of League of Ireland football as we head into the closing stages of the season as league titles, relegation fears and derby spoils are all on the agenda across both divisions.**

The Premier Division sees four fixtures take place on Friday while Derry City and Shamrock Rovers do battle on Sunday afternoon due to the latter's European commitments. The standout fixture across this gameweek is another installment of the Louth Derby with both teams in dire need of three points following some recent poor form. Drogheda United continue to linger in the relegation playoff spot, while Dundalk’s challenge for a top three finish has faded over the last month of results. Elsewhere in the Premier Division, there’s a clash of the in-form sides as St. Pats host Waterford at Richmond Park while Galway United can overtake Shelbourne in the table with a win at Eamon Deacy Park. Sligo Rovers will also travel to Dalymount Park to play Bohemians for the final time before its redevelopment as they go in search of their first league win for three months in their bid for survival.

The First Division also potentially holds some interesting storylines, as runaway leaders Cork City can be officially crowned champions if they overcome Wexford at Turners across accompanied by wins for Finn Harps away to UCD and Athlone Town at home to Bray Wanderers. Elsewhere in the division, a Munster derby takes place at Mounthawk Park as Kerry host Treaty United as they look to retain a push for a playoff finish for the first time in their history, while Cobh Ramblers and Longford Town who are both deadlocked on 40 points do battle at St. Colman’s Park with a playoff spot both fresh in the minds of both sides with just eight games left to play.
